title: I Sing the Mighty Power of God
story: Isaac Watts wrote this for his 1715 collection of songs for children, teaching them to see God's greatness written across creation and providence. Every hill, every flower, every cloud declares its Maker — for there is no place we can turn where God is not present, the whole earth being full of His care.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Holy, Holy, Holy
story: Reginald Heber, an Anglican clergyman who later became a missionary bishop in India, wrote this hymn for Trinity Sunday, echoing the ceaseless cry of the living creatures before God's throne in Revelation. Its adoration of the thrice-holy God — 'holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty' — has made it one of the church's most exalted anthems of worship.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Great Is Thy Faithfulness
story: Thomas Chisholm was a Kentucky schoolteacher and later an insurance agent whose health was frail and whose life held no great drama. Precisely there was the point: reflecting on God's steadfast mercies morning by morning, and on the words of Lamentations 3, he wrote of a faithfulness as sure as the sunrise and the changing seasons. He sent the poem to musician William Runyan, who set it to music, and it became one of the most beloved testimonies of God's daily care.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: His Eye Is on the Sparrow
story: Civilla Martin wrote this hymn after visiting a bedridden woman who, though ill for years, radiated joy. When Civilla asked the secret of her hope, the woman answered, 'His eye is on the sparrow, and I know He watches me.' That simple confidence — that the God who marks the fall of a sparrow surely cares for His children — became the heart of the song.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
story: Martin Luther, the reformer who stood almost alone against the might of church and empire, drew this hymn from the forty-sixth Psalm — 'God is our refuge and strength.' Written in a time of plague and peril, it became the battle-anthem of the Reformation, sung by those who trusted that though devils filled the world, 'one little word' of God should fell them.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: There’s a Wideness in God’s Mercy
story: Frederick Faber, an English clergyman, wrote hymns so his people would have songs of their own to sing. This one exults that God's mercy is 'wider than the sea,' and gently rebukes us for so often making His love narrower than it truly is by the hardness of our own reckoning.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Amazing Grace
story: John Newton spent his young manhood in the African slave trade, a coarse and profane sailor who mocked the faith of his godly mother. On a night in 1748 a violent storm nearly sank his ship, and in terror he cried out to God for mercy — a moment he marked ever after as the beginning of his conversion. He left the sea, became a pastor at Olney, and wrote this hymn out of his own astonishment that grace could save 'a wretch like me.' To the end of his life he said, 'I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Saviour.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Doxology
story: Thomas Ken, an English bishop known for his courage before kings, wrote three hymns for the students of Winchester College to sing morning, evening, and at midnight. Each closed with the same stanza of praise — 'Praise God, from whom all blessings flow' — and that closing verse, sung the world over to the tune 'Old Hundredth,' became the church's best-known doxology.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: God Will Take Care of You
story: Civilla Martin wrote these words during an illness, encouraged by her husband's confidence that God would provide. Assured that through days of toil, when heart doth fail, and every path, God would care for His own, she penned the refrain that has steadied countless anxious hearts: 'God will take care of you.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Savior, Like a Shepherd Lead Us
story: Long attributed to Dorothy Thrupp, this hymn first appeared in her 1836 hymnbook for children. It is a tender prayer to the Good Shepherd to lead, feed, guard, and keep His little flock, who are His and He is theirs.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: How Firm a Foundation
story: First published in 1787 in John Rippon's hymnal, its author is known only by the single initial 'K.' The hymn is built almost entirely on the promises of God to His people — 'Fear not, I am with thee' — a foundation that cannot be shaken however fierce the trial.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Standing on the Promises
story: R. Kelso Carter, a minister and teacher of frail health, came to rest his whole life upon the promises of Scripture rather than upon his feelings. Out of that settled confidence he wrote this marching hymn — that the believer stands secure on the sure and steadfast word of God.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Alas! and Did My Savior Bleed
story: Isaac Watts wrote this hymn marveling that the Sovereign Lord would die for such a one as he. It was being sung one night in a New York mission when the blind Fanny Crosby, long seeking peace, finally gave herself to Christ at the words 'Here, Lord, I give myself away' — and her darkness, she said, was flooded with light.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Our Great Savior
story: J. Wilbur Chapman, a Presbyterian evangelist who labored alongside Dwight Moody, wrote this hymn of Jesus as the friend of sinners. He is a Savior who loves, who saves, who keeps, and who satisfies the longing of the soul as nothing else can.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: When I Survey the Wondrous Cross
story: Isaac Watts, the father of English hymnody, wrote this meditation for a communion service, fixing the worshiper's gaze on the crucified Christ. Contemplating such love and sorrow flowing down from the cross, he could only conclude that the whole realm of nature, were it his to give, would be a present far too small — 'love so amazing, so divine, demands my soul, my life, my all.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: There Is a Fountain
story: William Cowper was a gifted poet who battled crushing depression and despair for much of his life, at times sinking near madness. Yet clinging to the fountain of Zechariah 13, 'opened for sin and for uncleanness,' he wrote of a fountain filled with blood where sinners lose all their guilty stains — and, like the dying thief, rejoiced to see it.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Christ the Lord Is Risen Today
story: Charles Wesley wrote this Easter hymn for the first service in the Wesleyans' new London chapel, a converted iron foundry, in 1739. Its ringing 'Alleluias' — added later to fit the tune — have made it the church's great anthem of the Resurrection.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Rock of Ages
story: Augustus Toplady, an English clergyman, wrote this hymn pleading refuge in the cleft 'Rock of Ages' — the wounded, crucified Christ in whom the sinner hides. A cherished tradition holds that he sheltered from a storm in a cleft of rock in Burrington Combe and there conceived the image, though this is more likely legend than documented fact; what is certain is the hymn's cry that nothing in our hands we bring, simply to His cross we cling.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: And Can It Be That I Should Gain
story: Charles Wesley wrote this hymn within days of his conversion in May 1738, overwhelmed that the immortal Son of God should bleed and die for him. Its wonder rises to a prisoner set free — 'my chains fell off, my heart was free, I rose, went forth, and followed Thee.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Blessed Assurance
story: The blind hymn-writer Fanny Crosby was visiting her friend Phoebe Knapp, who had composed a new melody and asked, 'What does this tune say to you?' Fanny listened and answered at once, 'Why, that says, Blessed assurance, Jesus is mine!' Within minutes the words were complete — a settled confidence in salvation from a woman who, though sightless from infancy, said she would not have it otherwise, since the first face she would ever see would be her Saviour's.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: The Solid Rock
story: Edward Mote grew up in London with no Christian upbringing — he later said his parents left him so untaught that he knew nothing of God. Converted as a young man, he became a cabinetmaker and then a pastor. One morning the phrase 'on Christ the solid rock I stand' came to him as he walked to work, and by the day's end he had written a hymn confessing that every other ground — feelings, frames, merit — is sinking sand.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: A Child of the King
story: Harriet Buell, musing after a Sunday service that though she owned little in this world she was the daughter of the King of kings, wrote 'My Father is rich in houses and lands.' The hymn celebrates the believer's title as an heir of God — a child of the King.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Take Time to Be Holy
story: William Longstaff, a wealthy Englishman devoted to Christian work, was stirred by an appeal to holiness — 'be ye holy, for I am holy.' He wrote this counsel to make time, amid a hurried world, for communion with God; for only those much with the Lord grow to be like Him.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: When We All Get to Heaven
story: Eliza Hewitt, a Philadelphia schoolteacher whose health was often broken, wrote joyful hymns fixed on heaven's hope. This one looks past present trials to the day when the saints shall gather home — 'what a day of rejoicing that will be!'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Sweet Hour of Prayer
story: The words are attributed to William Walford, a blind English shopkeeper who, it was said, dictated the lines to a visiting minister for want of being able to write them himself. Whatever the exact circumstances, the hymn has drawn generations to the mercy seat, that 'sweet hour of prayer' that calls the burdened soul from a world of care.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Break Thou the Bread of Life
story: Mary Lathbury wrote this hymn for the summer Bible gatherings at Lake Chautauqua. As the Lord once broke the loaves beside the sea, she prayed He would break open to the seeking soul the bread of His truth within the Scriptures.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: ’Tis So Sweet to Trust in Jesus
story: Louisa Stead, her husband, and their little daughter were picnicking on a New Jersey beach when they saw a boy drowning. Her husband rushed in to save him and was himself pulled under and drowned before their eyes. Out of that grief, leaning wholly on God for herself and her child, Louisa wrote of the sweetness of simply trusting Jesus and taking Him at His word.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Trust and Obey
story: During a Dwight Moody campaign, a young man rose in a meeting and said, 'I am not quite sure — but I am going to trust, and I am going to obey.' The musician Daniel Towner wrote down the striking phrase and passed it to John Sammis, who built from it this hymn: that there is no other way to be happy in Jesus but to trust and obey.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Have Thine Own Way, Lord
story: Adelaide Pollard longed to go to Africa as a missionary but could not raise the funds, and she grew discouraged with God. At a prayer meeting she heard an older woman pray, 'It's all right, Lord — just have Your own way with us.' The words struck her; meditating that night on the potter and the clay of Jeremiah 18, she wrote her surrender: 'Have Thine own way, Lord... Thou art the potter, I am the clay.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Grace Greater Than Our Sin
story: Julia Johnston, who taught Sunday school and wrote mission studies for many years, penned this hymn on the marvelous, matchless grace of God — grace that is greater than all our sin, freely bestowed upon all who believe.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Count Your Blessings
story: Johnson Oatman Jr., one of the most prolific gospel songwriters of his generation, offered in this hymn a simple, sturdy remedy for discouragement: when tempest-tossed and burdened, name your blessings one by one, and see what God has done.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: It Is Well with My Soul
story: Horatio Spafford, a Chicago lawyer, lost much of his fortune in the great fire of 1871. Two years later he sent his wife and four daughters ahead to Europe; their ship collided with another and sank, and all four girls drowned. His wife's telegram read simply, 'Saved alone.' Crossing the same ocean to join her, Spafford was shown the place where his daughters died, and there he penned the words, 'When peace, like a river, attendeth my way... it is well with my soul.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Stand Up, Stand Up for Jesus
story: The young minister Dudley Tyng preached to thousands in Philadelphia, and days later was fatally injured in a farm accident. As he lay dying he sent a final message to his fellow ministers: 'Tell them to stand up for Jesus.' His friend George Duffield preached the next Sunday on those words and closed with a poem he had written — 'Stand up, stand up for Jesus, ye soldiers of the cross.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Yield Not to Temptation
story: Horatio Palmer said this hymn came to him nearly complete while he was at work on a dry piece of music theory; the thought pressed so strongly that he laid everything aside to write it down. Its counsel is plain — fight manfully onward, for each victory will help you some other to win.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: He Leadeth Me
story: Joseph Gilmore, a young minister, was speaking at a Philadelphia prayer meeting on the twenty-third Psalm and found himself dwelling on the thought of God's leading. Afterward, still turning the idea over, he jotted the words on the back of a paper and handed them to his wife. Without his knowing, she sent them to a magazine, and only later did he discover his hymn already in print and being sung.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Near to the Heart of God
story: Cleland McAfee was a pastor whose two little nieces died of diphtheria in a single day. Grieving, he wrote this hymn of a quiet place near the heart of God, and that evening stood outside their quarantined home and sang it softly to his sorrowing brother's household through the door. It has comforted the bereaved ever since.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Rescue the Perishing
story: Fanny Crosby, ministering among the poor at a New York rescue mission, spoke one night on the lost and afterward could not rest until a certain young man was reconciled to God. The phrase 'rescue the perishing' had been given her as a theme, and from that evening's burden she wrote the hymn — a summons to lift up the fallen and tell them of a Saviour's mercy.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Take My Life, and Let It Be
story: Frances Ridley Havergal, an English poet of frail health and deep devotion, spent a night in a home full of people she longed to see brought closer to Christ. Before morning she saw her prayers answered, and in overflowing joy she wrote a consecration of every part of herself — hands, feet, voice, silver and gold, will and heart — 'take my life, and let it be consecrated, Lord, to Thee.'
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Blest Be the Tie That Binds
story: John Fawcett, a pastor of a small and poor English congregation, accepted a call to a larger church in London. The wagons were loaded to move, but as his weeping people gathered to say farewell, he and his wife could not bear to leave them. He unloaded the wagons, stayed, and soon after wrote this hymn to the love that binds Christian hearts together.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Living for Jesus
story: The melody came first: composer Harold Lowden wrote the tune and asked Thomas Chisholm to supply words to fit it. Chisholm answered with this hymn of wholehearted consecration — 'living for Jesus a life that is true,' surrendering all to the One who died to redeem him.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Nothing Between
story: Charles Albert Tindley, son of a slave, taught himself to read and rose from poverty to pastor a great Philadelphia congregation. His hymns sprang from a hard-won faith; this one pleads that nothing — worldly pleasure, habits, or pride — be allowed to come between the soul and its Savior.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing
story: Charles Wesley wrote this hymn near the anniversary of his conversion, longing that a thousand tongues might join to praise his Redeemer. Tradition holds the opening line was sparked by a remark of his mentor Peter Böhler, who said that had he a thousand tongues he would praise Christ with them all. It stands first in the Methodist hymnbook as a fitting call to worship.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Am I a Soldier of the Cross
story: Isaac Watts wrote this hymn to be sung after a sermon on 1 Corinthians 16:13, 'Quit you like men, be strong.' It challenges the believer not to expect to be carried to the skies 'on flowery beds of ease' while others fought to win the prize.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: Work, for the Night Is Coming
story: Anna Coghill wrote these words as a young woman, drawing from the Lord's saying that the night comes when no man can work. The hymn is a call to labor faithfully through life's short day while the light lasts, until the day is done and work is over.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul

title: On Jordan’s Stormy Banks
story: Samuel Stennett, an English Baptist minister, wrote this hymn of the pilgrim standing on Jordan's stormy bank and casting a wishful eye toward Canaan — the fair and happy land of promise beyond death, where the saints are ever blessed.
source: Robert J. Morgan, Then Sings My Soul
